pos: n. (Matthias of Janov, c. 1350–1393, master of Paris, Prague preacher, author of the Rules of the Old and New Testament)
etymology: Janov, a Bohemian place-name, a village of John; Matthias, from Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD.
biblical_def: Matthias of Janov was a Bohemian priest who took his master's degree at Paris, served as a canon at Prague, and spent his last years writing the long work called the Rules of the Old and New Testament. It is the most important book written in Bohemia before Hus and it contains, twenty years early, most of what the Hussite movement would afterwards fight about. Its governing idea is that Scripture is the rule by which everything in the church is to be measured, and that what cannot be measured by it has been added. By that rule he condemned the multiplication of images, the traffic in relics, the invocation of saints, pilgrimages and the swollen apparatus of ceremonies, calling them a crust grown over the simple thing Christ instituted; he urged the frequent communion of the laity as the proper remedy for a cold church; and he described the corrupted hierarchy of his own day under the name of the mystical body of Antichrist, by which he meant not one man but a system that had taken Christ's place in the church. He was made to recant some of this in 1389 and submitted. He died in 1393, two years before Hus began to preach at Bethlehem chapel. The dictionary enters him because the Bohemian Reformation did not begin with a political quarrel; it began with a man applying a rule.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rule as that which is prescribed as a guide; a relic as the remains of a saint preserved as an object of veneration; and Antichrist as one who opposes Christ, or usurps his place.
webster_full: RULE, n. [L. regula.] That which is prescribed or laid down as a guide to conduct; a standard to which to conform, or by which to judge.
RELIC, n. [L. reliquiae.] That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, or of something belonging to him, preserved as an object of veneration.
ANTICHRIST, n. A great adversary of Christ; the man of sin; one who opposes Christ, or usurps his authority and place in the church.
CEREMONY, n. [L. caeremonia.] Outward rite; external form in religion; forms of civility; outward forms of state.
COMMUNION, n. [L. communio.] Fellowship; the act of partaking of the Lord's supper; mutual intercourse or union.

For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
corruption_summary: Prague writer whose Rules of the Old and New Testament set Scripture as the measure of the church twenty years before Hus preached.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption he named is the overgrowth: a church which had not denied the gospel in words but had buried it under additions, each of which had once been a devotion and had become a law. Images, relics, pilgrimages and the invocation of saints are the particulars; the principle is that whatever the church adds to what Christ instituted will in time be required, and what Christ instituted will in time be neglected. His own evidence was the plainest possible: a people kept from the cup at the Supper while the shrines of the city did a profitable trade.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the rule itself. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20) is a rule of measurement, and the Reformation's great recovery was not a new doctrine but the courage to apply it to the church's own practice. Matthias applied it, was made to recant in 1389, and submitted; the dictionary records the submission as a failure and the rule as the thing that outlived him.

pos: n. (Jakoubek of Stribro, called Jacobellus, c. 1375–1429, master of Prague who restored the cup to the laity in 1414)
etymology: Stribro, a Bohemian town, from Czech stribro, silver, the mining town; Jakoubek, a diminutive of Jakub, Jacob, from Hebrew Ya'aqob, a supplanter.
biblical_def: Jakoubek of Stribro was a master of the university of Prague, a colleague of Hus, and the man who did the one thing which gave the Bohemian Reformation its visible sign. In the autumn of 1414, while Hus was on his way to Constance, Jakoubek concluded from the words of the institution and from the usage of the ancient church that communion in both kinds belongs to all the faithful and not to the clergy alone, and he began to administer the cup to the laity in Prague. Hus, consulted in prison, agreed; the Council of Constance condemned the practice; and from that moment the chalice was the badge of the whole movement, painted on its banners and carved over its church doors. Jakoubek defended it in writing for the rest of his life, and he also drew from the same principle the communion of infants, which the Bohemians practised and no other church has kept. After Hus's death he was the chief theologian of the Prague party, holding the Four Articles firmly and resisting the Taborites' rejection of purgatory, images and the remaining ceremonies, so that he was a radical to Rome and a conservative to Tabor. He died in 1429. The dictionary enters him for the method: he went to the words of institution, found the cup given to all, and acted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chalice as a cup or bowl, particularly the communion cup; a laity as the people distinguished from the clergy; and institution as the act of establishing, an established law or rite.
webster_full: CHALICE, n. [L. calix.] A cup or bowl; particularly, a communion cup; the cup used in the administration of the Lord's supper.
LAITY, n. [Gr. the people.] The people, as distinguished from the clergy; the body of the people not in orders.
INSTITUTION, n. [L. institutio.] The act of establishing; that which is established or appointed; an ordinance or rite established by authority.
BOTH, adj. Two, considered as distinct from others, or by themselves; the one and the other.
BADGE, n. A mark, sign, token or thing by which a person is distinguished; a token of profession.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Prague master who restored the cup to the laity in 1414, against the Council of Constance, and made the chalice the badge of the Bohemian Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named is the withholding of the cup. Christ gave the bread and the cup to his disciples and said of the cup that they should all drink of it; the medieval church, from motives of reverence and of convenience, withdrew the cup from the people and then defended the withdrawal by the doctrine of concomitance, which argues that the whole Christ is received under either kind and therefore nothing is lost. The reasoning may be ingenious but it answers a question nobody asked. The institution is plain and the church's business is to administer it, not to improve it. “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16) treats the cup as the congregation's own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative one: in worship the church does what Christ commanded and does not add or subtract. The dictionary parts from Jakoubek on infant communion, which he drew from the same text and which the text will not bear, since the apostle requires that a man examine himself and so eat. Consistency in a principle does not excuse an inference the Scripture refuses.

pos: n. (Jan Zelivsky, died 1422, radical preacher of Prague at St Mary of the Snows, who led the crowd of the first defenestration)
etymology: Zelivsky, Czech, of Zeliv, the Premonstratensian house where he had been a canon; Jan, the Czech form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Jan Zelivsky was a former canon of Zeliv who became preacher at the church of St Mary of the Snows in the New Town of Prague, and for three years the most powerful man in the city. He preached daily to the artisans and the poor, in Czech, on the Apocalypse and the prophets, with the cup administered to all and the whole programme of the Four Articles pressed as a demand upon the magistrates. On the thirtieth of July 1419 he led a procession from his church to the New Town hall to require the release of imprisoned Hussites; the crowd forced the building, and the councillors were thrown from the windows to the pikes below. That act began the Hussite wars. For the next three years Zelivsky governed Prague through the assembly of the commons, appointed and removed its officers, and was accused by his enemies of doing by tumult what he could not carry by argument. The patrician party took him by a stratagem in March 1422 and beheaded him in the Old Town hall. The dictionary enters him as a necessary warning, because he is on the right side of the doctrinal question and on the wrong side of the means: a preacher of the word of God who built a political power on his own congregation and used a crowd as an instrument.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tumult as the commotion of a multitude; sedition as a factious commotion of the people; and zeal as passionate ardor in the pursuit of any object.
webster_full: TUMULT, n. [L. tumultus.] The commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion.
SEDITION, n. [L. seditio.] A factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration of justice.
ZEAL, n. [Gr. to boil.] Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, this ardor in human beings is a mixture of good and evil affections.
MULTITUDE, n. [L. multitudo.] A great number, indefinitely; a crowd or throng; the populace.
MAGISTRACY, n. The office or dignity of a magistrate; the body of magistrates.

Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Prague radical preacher who led the crowd of the first defenestration in 1419, governed the city by its commons for three years, and was beheaded in 1422.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the preacher who makes his pulpit a political engine and his congregation a crowd. Zelivsky's doctrine of the cup was right and his demand that public sin be punished was in the Four Articles; the means by which he pressed both was a mob at a town hall, and men were killed by it. “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) was fulfilled upon him within three years, by the same city. The dictionary does not treat this as an excess to be excused by the provocation. It treats it as the thing itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the preached word as the preacher's weapon. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the whole of the commission, and it is enough; it converted the Roman empire without a riot. A minister who concludes that the word is too slow and reaches for the crowd has stopped believing the doctrine he preaches about the power of the word, whatever he says in the pulpit.

pos: n. (Nicholas of Pelhrimov, called Biskupec, c. 1385–1459, elected bishop of the Taborites and author of their confession)
etymology: Pelhrimov, a Bohemian town named for a pilgrim, from Latin peregrinus; Biskupec, Czech, a little bishop, the nickname his office earned him.
biblical_def: Nicholas of Pelhrimov was a Bohemian priest who joined the Taborite movement at its beginning and was elected, in 1420, one of the seniors or bishops by whom that community ordered its ministry—an office without any canonical warrant, held by election of the priests and the people, which is precisely why it mattered. He was the Taborites' theologian for forty years. He drew up their confession, wrote a long chronicle of their proceedings, and defended their positions in the great disputations: that the Supper is a memorial in which Christ is received by faith and not a sacrifice offered by a priest, that purgatory, the invocation of saints, images and the mass of ceremonies are without warrant, that priests are to be chosen by the churches they serve, and that the Scriptures are the sole judge. He was one of the Hussite spokesmen before the Council of Basel in 1433. After Lipany broke the field armies he kept the Taborite churches together, refused the Compacts, and was imprisoned by George of Podebrady at Podebrady castle, where he died about 1459. The dictionary enters him because his doctrine of the Supper and of the call of ministers stands nearer to the 1689 Confession than anything else in the fifteenth century, and because he held it under arms and then under arrest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; a memorial as something that preserves the memory of a thing; and election as the act of choosing a person to an office.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; the acknowledgment of a belief before witnesses.
MEMORIAL, n. [L. memorialis.] Preservative of memory; that which preserves the memory of something; a monument; a record.
ELECTION, n. [L. electio.] The act of choosing; choice; the act of selecting one or more from others; the choice of a person to an office.
SACRIFICE, n. [L. sacrificium.] An offering made to God; the act of offering to a divinity; any thing consecrated and offered.
SENIOR, n. [L. senior.] A person older than another; one who is older in office; an elder.

corruption_summary: Elected Taborite bishop and theologian for forty years, who held a memorial doctrine of the Supper, refused the Compacts, and died a prisoner.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary must mark where it parts from him. Taborite teaching on the Supper, as he framed it, tended to a bare memorialism which left nothing but the remembrance; the Reformed doctrine confesses a memorial sign and seal in which Christ is truly present to the believer by faith and by the Spirit, and refuses both transubstantiation and the emptied symbol. The dictionary holds that middle ground deliberately, and names the Taborite extreme as an over-correction made in the heat of a right quarrel.

The principle to recover is the choice of ministers by the churches. “And when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) is the warrant, and Tabor acted on it when no bishop in Christendom would ordain its priests. Nicholas held an office that had no canon behind it and every reason in Scripture, and he was called a usurper for it by men whose own succession had produced three simultaneous popes within living memory.

pos: n. (Prokop Holy, called the Great, c. 1380–1434, priest and commander of the Taborite field armies, killed at Lipany)
etymology: Prokop, the Czech form of Procopius, from Greek prokope, a going forward, an advance; Holy, Czech, the shaven or bald, his by-name as a priest without a beard.
biblical_def: Prokop Holy was a married priest of the Taborite obedience who took command of the field armies after Jan Zizka's death in 1424 and held it for ten years. He was not a soldier by training and never claimed to be more than a priest in the field; he fought in no armour and bore no sword, and the wagon tactics he inherited he used better than the man who invented them. Under him the Hussites destroyed the crusading armies sent against Bohemia—at Usti nad Labem in 1426, at Tachov in 1427, and at Domazlice in 1431, where the imperial host broke and ran at the sound of the approaching wagons without a battle—and then carried the war outward into Saxony, Silesia, Hungary and Brandenburg in the raids the Czechs called the beautiful rides. Having made Bohemia unconquerable, he went to Basel in 1433 as the chief of the Hussite embassy and negotiated. The Compacts which followed split his own side: the Prague party and the Catholic lords made terms, the field armies would not, and at Lipany on the thirtieth of May 1434 Prokop was defeated and killed by a coalition of Bohemians. The dictionary records the whole arc, including the end, which is the lesson: an army raised to defend a confession became an interest of its own and was destroyed by the people it had defended.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crusade as a military expedition undertaken for the recovery of the Holy Land, or against heretics; a captain as a commander of a company; and a truce as a temporary cessation of hostilities.
webster_full: CRUSADE, n. [Fr. croisade, from a cross.] A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land; any expedition undertaken with a religious pretext.
CAPTAIN, n. [L. caput, a head.] A head or chief officer; the military officer who commands a company; a commander of troops.
TRUCE, n. [Sax. treow, faith.] A temporary cessation of hostilities, by agreement of the parties; a suspension of arms; a short peace.
WAGON, n. A vehicle moved on four wheels, and usually drawn by horses; used for the transportation of heavy commodities.
VICTORY, n. [L. victoria.] Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest.

corruption_summary: Taborite priest who commanded the Hussite field armies for ten years, broke three crusades, negotiated at Basel, and was killed by his own countrymen at Lipany.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine corruption is the one the Hussite wars illustrate: a standing army raised for a confession which becomes a body with interests of its own. By 1434 the field armies were a profession. They had been in arms for fifteen years, they lived off the country they defended and the countries they raided, and they could not be demobilised because their men had no other trade. That is why Lipany was fought by Bohemians against Bohemians, and why the party of the Four Articles was broken by the party of the Four Articles.

The principle to recover is the limit of arms in the cause of religion. “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31) concedes the preparation and denies it the credit. The dictionary allows the lawful defence of a land against invasion, which Bohemia had in 1426 and 1431; it denies that a confession is established by cavalry, and notes that the Hussite settlement which actually lasted was the one negotiated at a table, by the Judge of Cheb.

pos: n. (Peter Payne, called Engliš, c. 1380–c. 1455, English Wycliffite who fled to Bohemia and became a Hussite spokesman at Basel)
etymology: Payne, English, from Old French paien, a countryman and so a heathen, a common surname; Engliš, the Czech by-name given him, the Englishman.
biblical_def: Peter Payne was an Oxford man and a convinced Wycliffite who, when the English authorities began to hunt Lollards in earnest, left the country about 1414 and went to Prague, where Wycliffe's books were honoured and his own were useful. He was admitted a master of the university, married, and lived the rest of his life as a Bohemian. He is the clearest personal link between the two movements: the Hussites had their Wycliffe from Oxford scholars and Czech students, and Payne was the Oxford scholar in the room. He argued the Hussite case in the disputations at Prague, served the movement as a diplomat on embassies to Poland and Lithuania, and in 1433 was one of the four Hussite spokesmen before the Council of Basel, where he was given the third of the Four Articles to defend—that the clergy should be stripped of worldly dominion and property. He inclined to the Taborite side, was imprisoned for a time by a Catholic lord and ransomed, and died in Bohemia about 1455. The dictionary enters him because the Reformation was never a national movement, whatever every nation has since claimed. A doctrine held in Oxford travelled in a student's satchel to Prague, and a hundred years later came back to England by way of Wittenberg.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an exile as one banished from his country; dominion as sovereign authority; and an advocate as one who pleads the cause of another.
webster_full: EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country by authority; the person banished.
DOMINION, n. [L. dominium.] Sovereign or supreme authority; the power of governing; territory under a government.
ADVOCATE, n. [L. advocatus.] One who pleads the cause of another in a court of judicature; one who defends or vindicates.
EMBASSY, n. The message or public function of an ambassador; the person or persons sent as ambassadors.
SCHOLAR, n. [L. scholaris.] One who learns of a teacher; a man of letters; one who has learning.

corruption_summary: Oxford Wycliffite who became a Bohemian master and spoke for the Hussites at Basel on the stripping of the clergy of worldly dominion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption at issue in his article at Basel was clerical lordship: bishops holding counties, abbots holding armies, a priesthood that was also the greatest landowner in the kingdom. The Hussite complaint was not envy but order—that a man cannot feed a flock and farm a province, and that the wealth drew into the ministry exactly the men who should never be in it. “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) is the apostolic requirement, and a church whose preferments are worth fighting for in a royal court has made that requirement untestable.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that doctrine has no country. Modern writing on the Reformation is organised by nation, which is convenient and misleading. Payne's life shows the real shape of it: Oxford to Prague by way of a persecution, and Bohemian theology furnished with English books. The dictionary holds that the church is one across the nations and that the gospel is carried by refugees at least as often as by missions.

pos: n. (Jan Pribram, died 1448, master of Prague and leader of the conservative Utraquist party against the Taborites)
etymology: Pribram, a Bohemian mining town, from a Slavic root for a gate or a passage; Jan, the Czech form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Jan Pribram was a master of the university of Prague and for thirty years the ablest spokesman of the conservative wing of the Hussite movement. He held the Four Articles and the cup for the laity, and he held almost nothing else that the Taborites held. Against them he defended the real and substantial presence in the Supper in the received sense, the vestments and the Latin canon, prayers for the dead and the remaining ceremonies, and the proposition that the Bohemian church was a reformed part of the catholic church and not a new one. He wrote against the Taborite priests with great force and some malice, drew up lists of their errors for the use of the Catholic lords, and worked steadily for the settlement which became the Compacts of Basel—communion in both kinds conceded to Bohemia, and Bohemia returned to the obedience of Rome. He quarrelled with Rokycana, was driven from Prague and returned, and died in 1448. The dictionary enters him because he is the type of a figure who appears at every Reformation: the moderate who secures the one concession his people most want, and secures it by giving away everything else, and who sincerely believes that he has saved the movement rather than ended it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a compact as an agreement between parties; moderation as a restraint of violence, the keeping of a due mean; and compromise as a mutual agreement settling a dispute by concession.
webster_full: COMPACT, n. [L. compactum.] An agreement; a contract between parties or nations; a covenant or convention.
MODERATION, n. [L. moderatio.] Restraint of violent passions or indulgence of appetite; the state of keeping a due mean between extremes.
COMPROMISE, n. [L. compromissum.] A mutual promise or contract of two parties in controversy, to refer their differences to arbitrators; an amicable agreement by concession.
CONCESSION, n. [L. concessio.] The act of granting or yielding; the thing yielded; acknowledgment by way of yielding a point.
OBEDIENCE, n. [L. obedientia.] Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law; submission to authority.

To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: Prague master who defended the old ceremonies against the Taborites and worked for the Compacts, by which Bohemia kept the cup and returned to Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the trade Pribram made, and it is worth stating as a principle rather than as a complaint about one man. The Compacts gave Bohemia the chalice and took back the doctrine the chalice had been a sign of; the Bohemian church kept a ceremony and lost its claim that Scripture is the judge. “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) is the apostle's account of a very similar negotiation, and his answer to it was not an hour's concession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary will not caricature him. His case was that Bohemia alone could not stand against Christendom, that the war had ruined the country, and that a church cut off from the catholic church would become a sect. All three were plausible and the first two were true. The answer is that the question was never whether Bohemia could stand but whether the thing it was asked to concede was the truth; and that a man who settles a doctrinal quarrel by a formula each side may read its own way has not made peace but postponed the war.

pos: n. (Bohemian city on the German border, German Eger; where the Judge of Cheb was agreed in 1432)
etymology: Czech Cheb, German Eger, from the river Ohre, Latin Agara; the city grew about the imperial castle on the Bohemian frontier.
biblical_def: Cheb is a frontier city of north-western Bohemia, long an imperial possession, and it is remembered for an agreement rather than for a battle. By 1432 the Council of Basel had decided that the Hussites could not be destroyed and must be heard. The question was on what terms, and the terms were settled at Cheb in May of that year, in the document the Czechs call the Judge of Cheb. It provided that when the Bohemians came to Basel their cause should be tried, and that the judge in the disputation should be the law of God, the practice of Christ, of the apostles and of the primitive church, together with the councils and the doctors truly grounding themselves upon the same. That sentence is the most remarkable thing the fifteenth century produced. A general council of the Western church agreed, in writing, that the standard of judgment in a controversy of religion should be the Scriptures and the primitive practice, with councils and doctors admitted only so far as they are founded on them. The Hussites went to Basel the next year and argued the Four Articles under that rule. The dictionary enters Cheb because the rule is the Reformation's own rule, conceded eighty-five years before Wittenberg by the body that would afterwards deny it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a judge as one who decides a question in controversy; a standard as that which is established as a rule or model; and primitive as original, first, belonging to the beginning.
webster_full: JUDGE, n. [L. judex.] A civil officer invested with power to hear and determine causes; one who has skill to decide on the merits of a question.
STANDARD, n. That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure; a test by which other things are tried.
PRIMITIVE, adj. [L. primitivus.] Pertaining to the beginning or origin; original; first; as the primitive church.
DOCTOR, n. [L. doceo, to teach.] A teacher; one who has received the highest degree in a faculty; one of the fathers of the church.
COUNCIL, n. [L. concilium.] An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice, particularly of ecclesiastics.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
corruption_summary: Bohemian frontier city where the Council of Basel conceded in 1432 that Scripture and primitive practice should be the judge in the Hussite disputation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption the Judge of Cheb exposes is the one the Reformation afterwards had to fight in the open: the claim that the church's tradition and its councils are a standard alongside Scripture rather than under it. Basel conceded the right rule in order to get the Bohemians to a table, used it for one disputation, and abandoned it as soon as the political work was done; Trent, a century later, defined the opposite. The concession is therefore evidence, and the dictionary keeps it as evidence: the rule of Scripture over councils was not a Protestant invention but a Protestant recovery of something a council itself had been obliged to admit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one in the document's own words, which the dictionary states in the prophet's: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Doctors and councils are honoured witnesses and are not judges. A church which will not submit its own canons to that examination has told you in advance what it expects the examination to find.

pos: n. (Bohemian town on the Bavarian road, German Taus; where the crusading army of 1431 fled without a battle)
etymology: Czech Domazlice, from a Slavic personal name Domazl; German Taus is a contraction of the same, the town guarding the Bohemian forest passes.
biblical_def: Domazlice guards the road from Bavaria through the Bohemian forest, and in August 1431 it was the point at which the fifth and last crusade against the Hussites ended. A great army of the empire, said to have been the largest yet sent, crossed the frontier under the margrave of Brandenburg with the papal legate Cardinal Cesarini in the camp, and advanced to the town. Prokop the Great came up with the field armies, and the imperial host, hearing the Hussite wagons on the road and the hymn the Hussites sang as they came, broke before contact; the army dissolved, the camp and the guns were abandoned, and the legate escaped with difficulty. No battle was fought. It was the rout at Domazlice which convinced the Council of Basel that the Bohemians had to be negotiated with, and so led to the Judge of Cheb the following year and to the Compacts. The dictionary enters Domazlice for the plainest reason: it is the Reformation's nearest thing to Gideon's battle or to the night the Assyrian camp emptied. A professional army, superior in everything but conviction, heard a hymn and ran. The lesson is not that God will always do so, for he usually does not, but that the issue was never in the numbers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rout as the defeat and disorderly flight of an army; a panic as a sudden fright without a visible cause; and a host as an army, a great multitude.
webster_full: ROUT, n. [Fr. route.] The breaking or defeat of an army or band of troops, or the disorder and confusion of troops thus defeated and put to flight.
PANIC, n. [Gr. from Pan, whose terror was supposed to be sudden.] A sudden fright; particularly, a sudden fright without real cause, or terror inspired by a trifling cause.
HOST, n. [L. hostis.] An army; a number of men embodied for war; any great number or multitude.
LEGATE, n. [L. legatus.] An ambassador; particularly, a cardinal or bishop sent by the pope as his representative.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; a religious song sung in worship.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
corruption_summary: Bohemian frontier town where the last crusade against the Hussites broke and fled in August 1431 without a battle being fought.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the triumphalist one. A deliverance like Domazlice is a standing temptation to a church, which concludes from one rout that God is committed to its arms; the Hussites drew that conclusion and were destroyed by their own countrymen at Lipany three years later. The dictionary records the deliverance and refuses the inference. God gave Bohemia a great mercy in 1431 and withdrew it in 1434, and he was not inconsistent in doing so.

The principle to recover is in the psalm: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The dictionary also records the detail the chroniclers preserved, that what the imperial troops heard was singing. A church's psalmody is not a military asset and is not meant to be one; but it is the sound of a people who believe what they are saying, and armies have always been able to tell the difference.

pos: n. (Nicholas Drabik, 1588–1671, exiled Moravian Brethren minister whose false prophecies were published by Comenius and who was executed at Pozsony)
etymology: Drabik, a Moravian surname from drab, a foot-soldier or a retainer; Nicholas, from Greek Nikolaos, a conqueror of the people.
biblical_def: Nicholas Drabik was ordained with John Amos Comenius in the Unity of the Brethren, lost his church in the Habsburg settlement of Moravia after 1620, and spent fifty years as an exile in Upper Hungary, where he kept himself by trading in cloth and wine. From 1638 he claimed to receive revelations, and for thirty years he produced them: that the house of Habsburg would fall, that the Turk and the Transylvanian princes were the instruments appointed, that the Brethren would be restored to Moravia, with dates. The dates passed. Comenius, his old fellow-student, believed him, collected his revelations with those of two other visionaries, and published them as the Light in Darkness—the gravest error of a great man's life, which tied the hope of the scattered Brethren to a political prophecy and discredited their cause when it failed. Drabik was at last arrested, condemned by the Pozsony court in 1671, and beheaded at eighty-three. The dictionary enters him as a case to be studied rather than mocked. He was a genuine sufferer for the gospel, robbed of his church and his country, and his gift was for telling a broken people what they most wished to hear, which is what the false prophet's gift always is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prophecy as a foretelling of future events by inspiration; a vision as something imaginary supposed to be seen; and an enthusiast as one who imagines he has special revelations.
webster_full: PROPHECY, n. [Gr. to foretell.] A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come; in Scripture, a book of prophecies.
VISION, n. [L. visio.] Something imaginary; the apparent appearance of something which is not real; a supernatural appearance.
ENTHUSIAST, n. [Gr. inspired.] One who imagines he has special or supernatural converse with God, or special communications from him.
IMPOSTURE, n. [L. impostura.] Deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
DELUSION, n. [L. delusio.] A false belief; a misleading of the mind; the state of being deluded or imposed upon.
scriptures: When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.

Then the LORD said unto me, The prophets prophesy lies in my name: I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, neither spake unto them: they prophesy unto you a false vision and divination, and a thing of nought, and the deceit of their heart.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: Exiled Moravian minister who prophesied the fall of the Habsburgs for thirty years, was published and believed by Comenius, and was beheaded in 1671.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is prophecy falsely claimed, and Scripture gives the test without any appeal to the prophet's character or sufferings: “if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken” (Deu 18:22). Drabik's predictions carried dates and the dates failed, repeatedly, over thirty years, and the test was therefore applied and the answer was known long before the Hungarian court got hold of him. The dictionary is cessationist and holds the canon closed; it also notes that even a church which expected continuing revelation would have had to reject this man on the plain words of Deuteronomy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern form of the error is unchanged and the dictionary names it where it appears: the dated predictions of political collapse, the identification of a contemporary power with a figure in Revelation, the revelation that happens to promise a wronged people exactly what it wants. The judgment on Comenius is the hardest part of this entry and must be stated. A man of his learning and piety accepted and printed these things because he was in exile, his church was dying, and he could not bear it; grief is an explanation and not a defence, and “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1) is addressed to men in exactly his position.
